name: Wire contract — every event knows which machine it is about

tasks.task:
The event protocol assumes there is exactly one machine running agent sessions. It must become host-addressed, and it lands first because every other package builds against it.

This is a deliberate breaking change to a named set of events, not an additive one. Each of the following gains a host identifier, and every producer and consumer of it changes in this same group so nothing is left decoding an older shape:

- the spawned-chat event, carrying the machine the chat is pinned to, fixed for that chat's life
- the spawn request, where naming a machine is REQUIRED
- host presence online and offline, each naming the machine it describes
- the unauthenticated report, naming both the machine and the agent backend whose credential is missing or expired
- the folder-registry snapshot and its change push, each naming the machine whose filesystem they describe
- the directory-browse request and response, addressed to one machine at a time
- the model-catalogue request and response, where each returned entry additionally names the backend serving it and the response can carry a per-backend error list alongside the models that did resolve
- the terminal-open request, naming the machine the shell starts on
- the cross-chat spawn call, naming the machine the new chat is created on
- the cross-chat chat-listing response, where each listed chat names its machine
- chat state, which additionally carries the effective permission mode the next turn will use
- the greeting the server sends a surface on connect, which now carries every registered machine with its presence, its last self-description and its last per-backend account report, alongside the web-bundle hash it already carried

The existing single-backend account report is replaced by a per-backend one identifying machine and backend together, and the existing account-wide connect and disconnect frames are replaced by the per-machine, per-backend pair enumerated below.

Every host-scoped control any surface changes has a surface-originated frame here carrying the machine id — no exceptions, because a surface with no frame to send renders a read-only list instead and the setting becomes reachable from one surface and not another. The daemon-owned lists are paired: a snapshot and a change push outward, an edit frame inward. The folder registry is the case that was previously outward-only.

New frames to define:

- a machine's self-description: its id, its user-editable name, platform, architecture, daemon version, whether an update is available for it, its default permission mode, a count of its chats carrying a per-chat override, its last-used model (absent until it has one), whether it is the account's home machine, its provisioned agent backends (id, label, version, state) and its optional components (id, label, size in bytes, a state of not-installed / downloading / installed / failed, plus optional progress and error)
- surface to server: rename a machine; make a machine the account's home machine
- surface to a machine: set that machine's default permission mode; install or remove an optional component; apply an available daemon update now; add a project root to that machine's folder registry and remove one from it; connect one backend's credential on that machine, carrying an OPTIONAL token where omitting it means re-adopt whatever that backend already has there, and disconnect one backend's credential on that machine
- a machine to surfaces: live component-download progress carrying state, received and total bytes and an optional error
- surface to a machine: a per-chat settings frame carrying that chat's permission-mode override, where omitting the field CLEARS the override rather than meaning no change

Model is OPTIONAL at every spawn site — the surface spawn request and the agent's cross-chat spawn alike. The contract must not oblige any caller to supply one; resolving what a chat actually runs on belongs to the machine, not to the protocol.

What must NOT change, and must be regression-guarded: per-chat monotonic sequence numbering and which events carry a sequence at all; the deliberately opposite boundary conventions of the reconnect cursor (exclusive) and the history paging cursor (inclusive); idempotency on the pairing of chat and client-generated input id; which events are live-only and therefore never persisted or replayed — the streamed text chunks, the queue and dequeue notices, the input acknowledgement, and the new component-progress frame whose settled result lands on the machine's self-description instead; and the binary framing of audio. The client's own connect greeting gains an optional source commit and build instant for version reporting.

Unhappy paths belong here because this is the cheapest place to catch them: a spawn request naming no machine; a frame naming a machine that is not registered; a component operation naming a component that machine does not offer; a permission mode outside the set the backend accepts; an empty machine name; a folder-registry edit carrying an empty path; a credential operation naming a backend that machine does not have. Each is rejected by validation with the offending value named — never silently defaulted, dropped, or routed to whichever machine happens to be attached.

The contract ships as runtime validation and types together, and every consuming package compiles and decodes against it before this group is done.

name: Testing A1 (wire contract)

tests.behaviour: A spawn that names no machine, or an unknown one, is rejected by validation naming the offending value — never defaulted to whichever daemon is attached.
steps: Bring up the server with at least one real daemon registered, and find how a surface asks for a new chat on a named machine.
Attempt a spawn with the machine identifier absent entirely, and again with a syntactically valid but unregistered machine identifier.
Watch both the immediate response AND the daemon side: check whether any agent session was actually created on the attached daemon.
Repeat the same probe for any other host-scoped frame (a host setting, a folder edit, a component operation) using an unregistered machine id.
tests.expect: PASS = each attempt is refused by validation with an error that names the offending field/value (missing machine id / the unregistered id), and NO chat, folder change or host mutation is created anywhere. FAIL if the request is accepted, silently defaulted to the only/attached daemon, coerced to a default machine, or if it errors generically without naming what was wrong. A rejection observed only in unit tests of the schema does NOT count — the rejection must be observed against the running server/daemon, and the absence of a side-effect must be positively checked (listing chats afterwards), not inferred from the error alone.

tests.behaviour: A chat is pinned to the machine named at spawn and every event about that chat carries that machine identifier for its whole life.
steps: Run TWO real daemons (two distinct registered machines) against one server simultaneously.
Spawn a chat naming machine B while machine A is also online, send it a turn that produces messages/tool activity, and capture the full event stream a surface sees.

Verify the machine identifier on the spawned event and confirm the work actually ran on B (e.g. by a turn whose output is machine-distinguishing, such as the working directory or hostname visible on B only).
Reconnect a surface and replay the chat; confirm the machine identity is still B and unchanged.
tests.expect: PASS = the spawned event carries B, the turn demonstrably executed on B (evidence from B's own filesystem/process, not just the event's own field), and the pinning survives reconnect/replay. FAIL if the chat runs on A, if any consumer has to infer the host from 'the daemon that happens to be connected', or if the machine field is absent/empty on any chat-scoped event. A single-daemon run does NOT satisfy this test — with only one daemon online, correct routing is indistinguishable from routing to whatever is attached.

tests.behaviour: The greeting the server sends a surface on connect enumerates every registered machine with presence, last self-description, and last per-backend account report, alongside the web-bundle hash.
steps: With two daemons registered — one online, one deliberately stopped — connect a fresh surface client to the server and capture the server's reply to the connect frame.
Inspect the reply for the list of machines: for each, its presence/last-seen, its cached self-description, and its cached per-backend credential report; and for the bundle hash it already carried.
Change something on a live machine (e.g. its name or a component/credential state), then connect a SECOND, brand-new surface that was not connected when the change happened.
tests.expect: PASS = the greeting lists BOTH machines (including the offline one, marked not-online with its cached self-description and account report), carries the web-bundle hash, and the late-joining surface receives the post-change values from the greeting alone without having to ask. FAIL if the offline machine is omitted, if any of presence / self-description / per-backend account report is missing or is an account-wide (non-per-machine, non-per-backend) shape, or if the late surface only learns the state after a subsequent live push. Reading the server's cache directly does NOT count — the evidence must be the greeting frame actually received by a client.

tests.behaviour: Backend credentials are addressed per machine AND per backend: connect (with or without a token) and disconnect act on exactly one backend on one machine and are reported back per backend.
steps: On a real host with a real, logged-in agent backend, observe the account report a surface receives and confirm it identifies both the machine and the backend (not an account-wide 'connected' flag).
Disconnect that backend's credential on that machine, then re-connect it with the token field OMITTED (the re-adopt path), and observe the reports emitted after each action.
Verify the real side-effect on the host each time — the daemon's own credential store on disk actually emptied, then actually repopulated — and confirm a real turn can run afterwards.
Attempt a credential operation naming a backend that machine does not have, and (with two machines online) confirm an operation aimed at machine A leaves machine B's credential state untouched.
tests.expect: PASS = each report names machine+backend; disconnect demonstrably empties that host's credential store and connect-without-token demonstrably restores a working credential (proved by a real turn succeeding after re-connect, against the real backend); the unknown-backend operation is rejected naming the offending backend; machine B is unaffected. FAIL if any report is account-wide, if the state change is only reflected in an event with no on-host change, or if an unknown backend is accepted/ignored. A stubbed or in-memory credential store does NOT count — the real store on the real host must be observed changing, and the post-connect turn must reach the real agent backend.

tests.behaviour: The unauthenticated report names both the machine and the backend whose credential is missing or expired.
steps: Put one backend on one real host into a genuinely credential-less state (using the product's own disconnect path rather than editing internals, if possible).
Attempt to run a turn on that backend on that host and capture what surfaces receive.
With two machines online, confirm the report identifies which machine is affected and that the other machine's chats keep running.
tests.expect: PASS = an unauthenticated report is emitted carrying BOTH the machine identifier and the backend identifier, the turn is refused rather than hanging, and the unaffected machine keeps serving turns. FAIL if the report omits either identifier, if it is account-wide, or if the surface has to guess which host is logged out. Reconstructing this from log lines does NOT count — it must be the protocol frame a connected surface receives. If the state cannot be induced without destroying a credential that cannot be restored, report it as an environmental blocker rather than mocking it.

tests.behaviour: Each machine's folder registry is published per machine (snapshot + change push) and edited by machine-addressed inbound frames, with empty and non-existent paths refused.
steps: With two daemons online, connect a surface and capture the folder-registry snapshots — confirm each is attributed to a specific machine.
Add a real existing directory as a project root on machine A, then remove it, capturing what surfaces receive after each edit, and verify the daemon's own persisted registry on A actually changed.
Confirm machine B's published registry is untouched by the A edits, and that the same path string on B is a separate entry.
Attempt an edit carrying an empty path, and an edit carrying a path that does not exist on that machine.
tests.expect: PASS = a snapshot arrives per machine on connect, every add/remove produces a change push naming the edited machine, the on-disk registry of A reflects the edit, B is unchanged, and both the empty path and the non-existent path are refused with the offending value named. FAIL if the registry is outward-only with no inbound edit frame, if a push omits the machine identifier, if two machines' registries merge into one list, or if an invalid path is accepted/silently dropped. An event echo with no corresponding change in the daemon's persisted registry does NOT count as an add.

tests.behaviour: Directory browsing is addressed to one machine at a time and returns that machine's filesystem, refusing traversal outside its designated roots.
steps: With two daemons whose filesystems differ in a recognisable way (create a uniquely-named directory under a registered root on machine A only), issue a browse addressed to A and then the same browse addressed to B.
Confirm each response is attributable to the machine it was asked of, and that the listing content matches that machine's real filesystem (child directories only).
Attempt to browse a path that escapes the machine's designated roots (relative traversal or an absolute path outside them).
tests.expect: PASS = the A-addressed browse shows the uniquely-named directory and the B-addressed browse does not; each response carries/identifies its machine; and the escaping path is refused with a not-found style error rather than returning a listing of the root or home directory. FAIL if the browse resolves against the server's or the surface's own filesystem, if the machine cannot be named in the request, or if traversal outside the roots yields any listing. Comparing against a fixture directory tree does NOT count — the uniqueness marker must be created on the real host and observed only in that host's response.

tests.behaviour: The model catalogue is requested per machine and each returned entry names its serving backend; per-backend failures are returned alongside the models that did resolve.
steps: Ask a real, credentialed host for its model catalogue and inspect the response: entries, their ordering, and whether each entry names the backend that serves it.
Confirm the list came from a real provider read (models present that are not hard-coded in the repo — cross-check the source for a static list).
Induce a failure for one backend on a host that has at least one working backend (or, if only one backend exists, on a host whose credential is absent) and request the catalogue again.
Request the catalogue addressed to a second machine and confirm the response is attributed to the machine asked.
tests.expect: PASS = every entry names its backend, the response carries a per-backend error list, and in the induced-failure case the failing backend appears in the errors WHILE models from any backend that answered remain present in the same response. FAIL if entries lack a backend field, if a single backend failure empties or fails the whole response, if there is no error channel at all, or if the catalogue is a hard-coded list in the repo. A recorded/fixture provider response does NOT count — the models must come from the real provider over the real credential.

tests.behaviour: A terminal-open request names the machine and the shell genuinely starts on that machine.
steps: With two daemons online, open a terminal session naming machine A and run a command whose output uniquely identifies the host (hostname, or a file that exists only on A).
Repeat naming machine B and compare the outputs.
Attempt to open a terminal naming an unregistered machine.
tests.expect: PASS = the A session's output identifies A, the B session's identifies B, and the unregistered machine is refused naming it. FAIL if the machine cannot be named in the open request, if both sessions land on the same host, or if the session silently starts wherever the daemon connection happens to point. Verifying only that a ready frame came back does NOT count — you must observe host-distinguishing command output from inside the shell.

tests.behaviour: Cross-chat tool frames are host-addressed: an agent's spawn call names the machine to create on, and each entry of a chat listing names its machine.
steps: With two daemons online, drive a real agent turn in a chat on machine A that uses the cross-chat spawn capability targeting machine B.
Confirm the new chat was actually created on B (its work runs on B's filesystem) and that the frames a surface sees show the cross-chat activity with the target machine named.
Exercise the cross-chat chat-listing capability and inspect every returned entry for its machine identifier, with chats existing on both machines.
Check whether the cross-chat spawn can be made without naming a model.
tests.expect: PASS = the spawned chat lives on B with evidence from B itself, the listing attributes each chat to its own machine (chats on A and B distinguishable), and a spawn omitting the model succeeds. FAIL if the cross-chat spawn has no way to name a machine, if it lands on the caller's own host regardless, if listing entries are machine-less, or if the model is mandatory. Calling the underlying function directly in a unit test does NOT count — it must go through a real agent turn issuing the tool call over the live stack.

tests.behaviour: Chat state carries the effective permission mode for the next turn; a per-chat override can be set and is CLEARED by omitting the field; invalid modes are rejected.
steps: Read a chat's state on a live host and note the effective permission mode reported with no override in place; confirm it matches the machine's default.
Set the machine's default to a different accepted mode and confirm chats without an override report the new effective mode.
Set a per-chat override to a third accepted mode, confirm the chat's reported effective mode changes, then send the per-chat settings frame with the mode field OMITTED and re-read the state.
Attempt to set a permission mode value the backend does not accept, and attempt a machine rename with an empty name.
tests.expect: PASS = effective mode resolves override → machine default → the documented fallback and is visible on chat state; omitting the field on the per-chat settings frame CLEARS the override so the chat falls back to the machine default (it must NOT be treated as 'leave unchanged'); the invalid mode and the empty machine name are both refused with the offending value named. FAIL if chat state has no effective-mode field, if omission is a no-op, or if an out-of-set mode is accepted or silently coerced. Reading a config file does NOT count — the effective mode must be observed on the chat-state frame a surface receives.

tests.behaviour: Each machine publishes a complete self-description, and rename / set-home take effect from a surface-originated frame.
steps: Capture a live machine's self-description and check every advertised field is present and plausible: identifier, editable name, platform, architecture, daemon version, update-available flag, default permission mode, the count of its chats carrying a per-chat override, last-used model (may be absent before any catalogue read), home-machine flag, provisioned backends with id/label/version/state, and optional components with id/label/size/state.
Rename the machine from a surface and confirm a fresh self-description carries the new name and that it persists across a daemon restart.
Give one chat on that machine a permission-mode override and confirm the override count in the self-description moves; clear it and confirm it moves back.
With two machines registered, make the second one the account's home machine and confirm exactly one machine reports the home flag afterwards.
tests.expect: PASS = every listed field appears (last-used model may be legitimately absent only on a machine that has never read a catalogue), rename survives a daemon restart, the override count tracks real per-chat overrides, and setting home moves the flag so exactly one machine holds it. FAIL if any field is missing or hard-coded, if the override count is static, if renaming requires editing a file on the host, or if two machines simultaneously claim home. Values asserted from a schema/type definition rather than from a live emitted description do NOT count.

tests.behaviour: Optional components are installed/removed per machine with live progress frames, and the settled result lands on that machine's self-description.
steps: Read a machine's advertised optional components and their states.

Trigger an install of one component on that machine from a surface and observe the live progress frames while it runs — check they carry the machine, the component, a state, and received/total byte counts that actually advance.
Let it settle, then confirm the component's installed state appears on the machine's self-description AND the payload really exists on that host's disk at roughly the advertised size.
Remove it and confirm both the on-disk removal and the state change; then attempt an install naming a component that machine does not offer.
tests.expect: PASS = progress frames stream with advancing byte counts, the settled state is reflected on the self-description (not only on the transient progress frame), the real bytes appear on and later disappear from the host's disk, and the unknown component id is refused naming it. FAIL if progress is synthetic/instant, if the settled state only lives on the progress frame, if nothing lands on disk, or if an unoffered component id is accepted. If the download cannot complete for a genuine environmental reason (no network egress to the weights host, insufficient disk), report it as an environmental blocker — do not substitute a stub download.

tests.behaviour: Regression: per-chat sequence numbering stays monotonic, and the live-only events (streaming text chunks, queue/dequeue notices, input acknowledgement, component progress) are never persisted or replayed.
steps: Drive a real chat through a turn that produces streaming text, a queued-then-running second input, and an input acknowledgement; capture the complete live event stream.
Check the sequence numbers on the events that carry them are strictly increasing per chat and that the live-only event kinds carry no sequence of their own.
Disconnect the surface, reconnect and replay the chat from the beginning, and also fetch the chat's history through the non-WebSocket path.
Trigger a component-download progress frame, then replay/refetch and check whether it reappears.
tests.expect: PASS = sequences are per-chat monotonic with no gaps introduced or duplicates; on replay and on history fetch the finalised messages appear exactly once and NONE of the streaming chunks, queue/dequeue notices, input acknowledgements or component-progress frames reappear. FAIL if any live-only event is replayed or persisted, if a live-only event has acquired its own sequence number, or if replay duplicates a message. Inspecting a persistence module's code does NOT count — the check must be on the actual replayed/refetched stream.

tests.behaviour: Regression: the reconnect cursor is exclusive and the history paging cursor is inclusive — the two boundaries stay deliberately opposite.
steps: Build a chat with several sequenced events and note a specific event's sequence number, N.
Request a reconnect-style replay using N as the cursor and record which events come back relative to N.
Request the paged history through the HTTP-style path using N as the cursor and record which events come back relative to N.
Also exercise the documented 'give me everything' value for each path and confirm nothing at the very start of the chat is skipped.
tests.expect: PASS = the replay returns strictly events after N (N itself excluded) while the history fetch returns N itself and later (inclusive), and each path's full-history value genuinely returns the first event of the chat. FAIL if both cursors behave the same way, if either is off by one, if the 'everything' value skips the first event, or if someone has 'aligned' the two conventions. Asserting from documentation or type comments does NOT count — both requests must be issued against the live stack and their returned sequence numbers compared.

tests.behaviour: Regression: input idempotency is keyed on the pairing of chat and client-generated input id.
steps: Send the same user input twice to one chat with an identical client-generated id (simulating a retry), and observe both the acknowledgements and the chat's resulting messages.
Send an input with the same client-generated id but to a DIFFERENT chat.
Send two genuinely distinct inputs with distinct ids and confirm both land.
Confirm the outcome in the chat's persisted history after a replay, not just in the live stream.
tests.expect: PASS = the duplicate produces exactly one user turn in the chat (in live stream and in replayed history), the same id reused on a different chat is NOT suppressed, and distinct ids both land. FAIL if the duplicate creates two turns, if the second one errors loudly instead of being quietly dropped, or if the id is treated as globally unique across chats. Checking only that the same acknowledgement came back twice does NOT count — the message count in replayed history is the evidence.

tests.behaviour: Regression: the audio session's framing is unchanged — control frames textual, mic and TTS payloads binary, nothing sequenced or replayed.
steps: Open a real audio session against a live host using the product's own session-opening path and capture the frames on the wire.
Confirm the control frames are the textual kind and the mic/TTS payload frames are binary, in the documented sample formats.
Confirm no audio frame carries a sequence number and that replaying the chat afterwards returns no audio frames.
Attempt to open a session whose identifying details do not match the token it presents.
tests.expect: PASS = binary payload frames observed as binary on the wire (not base64 inside a text frame), control frames textual, zero audio events in any replay, and the mismatched session refused. FAIL if audio payloads have become text-encoded, if any audio frame gained a sequence number, if audio shows up in replay, or if a mismatched session is accepted. If the voice path cannot be opened because a genuinely-absent credential or missing local speech component blocks it, report an environmental blocker — do not substitute a fake audio client.

tests.behaviour: A client's connect greeting may carry its source commit and build instant, and the server surfaces them for version reporting.
steps: Connect a client that supplies the optional source-commit and build-instant fields, and a second client that omits them entirely.
Confirm both connections are accepted and neither is rejected for the presence or absence of those fields.
Find where the server exposes connected-client versions and confirm the supplied commit and build instant are visible there for the first client.
tests.expect: PASS = both clients connect successfully, and the reported commit/build instant for the supplying client match exactly what it sent. FAIL if the fields are mandatory, if supplying them is rejected, if they are accepted but discarded with no way to read them back, or if the value read back is a placeholder/hard-coded string. Finding the fields in a type definition does NOT count — the round trip through the live server must be observed.

tests.behaviour: Model is optional at every spawn site and resolves on the machine, including the error when a machine has never read a catalogue.
steps: Spawn a chat from a surface naming a machine but no model, on a host that has successfully read a catalogue, and confirm the turn actually runs.
Determine which model it ran on and confirm it is the machine's last-used/most-recent-catalogue choice rather than a value the surface supplied or a hard-coded constant.
Spawn a further chat naming an explicit model from that machine's catalogue and confirm the chat runs on it and that the machine's last-used value follows the machine (visible from another surface).
Attempt a model-less spawn on a machine that has never successfully read a catalogue (e.g. one whose backend credential is not connected).
tests.expect: PASS = model-less spawns succeed and run on the machine-resolved model at both spawn sites (surface spawn and the agent's cross-chat spawn), last-used tracks the machine not the surface, and the no-catalogue-yet machine refuses a model-less spawn with an error saying exactly that. FAIL if any spawn path requires a model, if the surface's default is what gets used, or if the no-catalogue case silently falls back to a hard-coded model. A chat that is created but never produces a real agent turn does NOT count as a successful spawn.

tests.behaviour: The contract ships as runtime validation and types together, and every consuming package builds and decodes against the new host-addressed shapes with no legacy shapes left behind.
steps: Build/typecheck the whole workspace from a clean state and run the repo's own test suites for the wire contract and its consumers.

Search the consuming packages for any remaining decode/producer path using the pre-change, non-host-addressed shapes of the named events — in particular the replaced account-wide credential report and the replaced account-wide connect/disconnect frames.
Feed the live stack a frame in one of the old, host-less shapes and observe how it is handled.
Confirm the host identifier is genuinely required (not optional-with-default) in the validation for the events the task lists as breaking changes.
tests.expect: PASS = clean build and green suites with no type errors or skipped packages; no consumer still emits or accepts the superseded account-wide shapes; an old-shape frame is rejected by validation rather than accepted-and-ignored; and the host identifier is required rather than defaulted. FAIL on any build/type error, on a leftover legacy decode path, on an old-shape frame being tolerated, or on the host field being optional with an implicit default. Disabling, skipping or loosening a check to make the build pass does NOT count as a pass — report it as a failure.

name: Daemon distributable — artifact, installer, OS service, first run

tasks.task:
The daemon stops being a container and becomes something a person installs on a machine that has nothing on it but an operating system.

Produce an installable artifact per operating system and architecture — macOS on both architectures and Linux on both — each carrying one bundled program file, a pinned language runtime, the platform's prebuilt native addons (currently only the one the voice-activity model needs), the voice-activity model file itself (~2 MB, the one model weight in the artifact, so end-of-utterance detection and barge-in work on every machine with nothing downloaded), and an installer. The artifact is signed with the project's own signing identity, which is what the self-update path later verifies against. It must install and run on a machine with no toolchain, and it must report its version, its source commit and its build instant.

There are two ways in. One is a single shell command a person pastes into any machine with a shell. The other is from a surface, which the surface groups own; what this group owes them is an install that works when it is run. First run is self-contained: the installer registers the daemon with the machine's own service manager — launchd on macOS, a user-level systemd unit on Linux — with restart-on-failure and start-at-boot, then asks for the pairing code the user takes from an already-linked surface and submits it with the daemon's public key. The code is minted by the server when a linked surface asks for it, and rendered by that surface; the installer redeems it and mints nothing. Before it registers anything, the installer states once, plainly, what the daemon will be able to do on that machine: it runs as that user, with that user's whole authority.

The daemon runs as the invoking user under that user's home, so the agent reads that user's own configuration and a chat behaves the way that user's agent behaves in their own terminal. The install writes the command-line skill that ships in the artifact into that user's own agent skills directory, and rewrites it on every self-update, so every chat on the machine can drive the command line and the skill matches the daemon it describes. It survives logout, surface disconnects, and any application on that machine closing. Everything it keeps for itself lives under that user's own patch directory, resolved from that user's home and nothing else: its local control socket, its per-chat state, and, on the account's home machine, the three special threads' working folders. The service unit therefore carries no working directory of its own, and none of these paths is configurable.

Re-running the installer on a machine that is already registered re-uses what is already stored rather than creating a second machine. A machine whose registration has been revoked pairs again from scratch.

What must NOT be inside the artifact: the agent backend, the language environment the voice components need, and any model weights large enough to be an optional per-machine download — today the speech synthesiser's and the local transcriber's. Those are provisioned on the machine after install, and carrying them would put multiple gigabytes into every install ahead of any use of voice. The voice-activity model passes that size test rather than failing it — two megabytes, and every machine needs it — so it ships in the artifact as listed above.

Prove the claim rather than asserting it: the artifact must be shown installing and running on a bare machine carrying only an operating system.

Unhappy paths: an artifact for the wrong platform refuses rather than half-installing; a service that fails to register says why rather than leaving something that runs once and is gone at reboot; an install on a machine that cannot reach the server still leaves a registered service and says the code could not be submitted, so a fresh code can be entered once the server is reachable; a code the server rejects as expired or already used is reported by the installer as exactly that.

name: Testing A2 (daemon distributable)
Every trigger ingress gated, because a turn carries the machine's authority

tasks.task:
A turn now runs on a real machine with the host user's full authority, including elevated commands where that user has them. Every path by which something outside patch can cause a turn to run is an entry point to that authority, and each must be authenticated or gated by an unguessable secret before anything is dispatched.

Audit and close each one: inbound webhooks and their signature schemes, the calendar push subscription, the task-manager integration, the messaging-bot endpoint with its single allowed sender, and the schedule ticker. Verification happens before any chat is spawned or messaged, never after. A rejected inbound produces no run, is logged as rejected with its reason, and is visible in the inbound log a person can read back. Signature failures, unknown job ids and unexpected senders are rejections, not warnings.

The daemon's local control socket is owner-only and additionally carries a bearer key that the daemon alone mints, on each start, keeping it beside the socket in its own directory at owner-only permissions. The tool child each query launches is handed the current value in its environment; the command line a person runs on that machine reads it from that file. Same user, same machine remains the real boundary; the key closes the case where some other process on that machine can reach the socket. The tool child is still identified by the environment the daemon set for it, not by the key it presents.

Unhappy paths: an inbound naming a job that does not exist; an inbound whose signature does not verify; a message from a sender who is not the allowed one; a caller of the local socket presenting no key or the wrong one; an inbound arriving faster than it should be accepted. Each is refused with nothing dispatched, and each leaves an audit line.

name: Testing A3 (trigger ingress authority)
Server — a relay for any number of machines

tasks.task:
The server holds exactly one daemon socket today and closes the older one when a second attaches. It must become a relay for any number of machines, all of them peers.

The registry keeps a record per machine — its id, its user-editable name, its platform, its version and its last-seen state — and any number may be registered. A daemon dials in and authenticates as itself; a second, third and fourth attach alongside rather than displacing each other, each holding its own live link.

Every chat records the machine it belongs to, and the server routes that chat's events to that machine alone. A surface event for a chat goes to that chat's machine; an event from a machine fans out to the account's surfaces carrying the machine it came from. Presence is tracked and published per machine, so one machine going away says nothing about the others.

Everything the server buffers is partitioned per machine: surface input for an offline machine, and payloads produced by fired triggers, are held against that machine and flushed when that machine reconnects, bounded exactly as they are today. When a machine's link drops, only that machine's in-flight chats resolve to a visible error naming it; chats on other machines are untouched.

The server caches each machine's last self-description and its last per-backend account report and replays them, along with every machine's presence, in the greeting it sends a surface on connect — so a surface that connects after a machine dropped shows it as offline immediately, with no window in which the app claims everything is fine.

The routes that were single-daemon become machine-addressed: the link-liveness check answers for one named machine or returns a per-machine list, reporting healthy while any machine is up and unhealthy only when every one is down; the model catalogue and the folder-skill lookup are round-tripped to the named machine; chat creation carries the machine alongside the folder and an optional model.

Renaming a machine and marking a machine as the account's home machine are server-side operations that take effect for every surface.

Registration has one direction and this group owns its minting end: the server mints a single-use registration code when a linked surface asks for one, and redeems it when a daemon submits it with its public key, answering with that machine's own key and recording its self-description. Surfaces render that code and installers redeem it; neither mints one. A daemon submitting from a machine that is already registered gets its existing key back rather than a second machine.

A real daemon attaches to this server in its tests, which is what registration redeeming, per-machine routing and per-machine buffering are proved against. The claims that need a second machine attached at the same time are proved on the two-daemon rig (C1), where a second real machine identity first exists (18-tech-stack.md ## Testing).

Unhappy paths: a frame naming a machine that is not registered; a chat whose machine has been removed; two links claiming the same machine identity; a route called with no machine where the answer would be ambiguous. Each is a named error, never a silent pick of whichever machine happens to be attached.
