name: Testing B1 (server multi-host relay)
Server — daemon distribution, and the install command a surface shows

tasks.task:
The server becomes the place machines get their daemon from.

It serves the current artifact for each operating system and architecture together with a version manifest saying what the current build is. That one channel feeds two consumers: a brand-new machine's install, and every existing machine's self-update. Publishing a new build is what makes both see it.

The server is also the single source of the one-line install command a surface offers when the user adds a machine. A surface must NOT compose that command out of its own guesses about the server's address or the artifact's name: the server produces it, per target operating system, from the same manifest it serves the artifacts from, so the command a phone shows and the command the desktop shows are the same command and both point at the running server. Make that a first-class thing a surface retrieves by naming its target operating system, so a surface renders what the server hands back without knowing how a build is named.

Server and daemon versions move independently, and the event protocol is the compatibility contract between them: the server states the daemon version range it supports, and a machine outside that range is reported as needing an update rather than left to misbehave quietly.

Unhappy paths: an artifact requested for a platform that has no build; a manifest read while a publish is only half finished; a machine reporting a version the server does not support; a request for the install command before anything has been published. Each answers plainly rather than handing back something unusable.

name: Testing B2 (daemon distribution and install command)
Daemon — which machine am I, and the two-daemon test rig

tasks.task:
Each daemon must know and publish what machine it is, and stop behaving as though it lives in a container.

It has a stable machine id issued at registration and a name defaulted from the machine's own hostname and editable from any surface. It sends the self-description the wire contract defines on connect and again whenever anything in it changes, filling the fields it answers for itself: its name, its platform and architecture, its own version, and whether it is the account's home machine. Surfaces label it by that name rather than by its id.

It stops assuming a mounted filesystem and a container identity. It owns its own folder registry — the project roots the user designates plus folders seen in that machine's recent chats, filtered so that only real project folders are published and dot-directories and system scratch directories never are, while an explicitly designated root is always shown — and publishes that registry as its own, with its machine id on both the snapshot and every change push. Designating a root and dropping one are things it ACCEPTS rather than only reports: it takes the contract's add and remove frames from a surface and the matching endpoints on its own local socket, validates the path against its own filesystem, writes its registry and answers with the change push, so a graphical surface and the command line edit the same list by the same route.

Every host-scoped control the contract lets a surface change is also reachable on this machine's own local socket, one endpoint per frame and one implementation behind both, because the command line's default machine is the one it is invoked on and those commands must work there without a round trip through the server. That is the standing rule for this daemon: a host-scoped control the contract gains arrives with its socket endpoint in the same change. The one endpoint with no frame behind it is opening the five-minute voice-device adoption window, which is local-only because the daemon adopts the device itself. It answers directory-listing requests for its own tree, confined to its designated roots and refusing traversal out of them, fast enough that a picker feels instant. A folder path means nothing without the machine it is on: the same string on two machines is two different directories, and whether a folder exists is checked on the machine that will actually run the chat.

The shell it opens for a surface runs on it, in the folder asked for or — when none is named, which is a different and explicit request — in the first of its own project roots that exists, reporting back the directory it really started in. It uses the user's own version-control identity and configuration because it runs as that user, and it refuses to sit waiting on a credential prompt it has no terminal to answer.

Build the rig this whole change is proved on: one server with two real daemon processes attached at once, each with its own machine identity and its own home directory on the test machine, so per-machine routing, presence and buffering are exercised against real daemons rather than stand-ins (18-tech-stack.md ## Testing). The multi-machine claims the server makes are proved here, because this is the first point at which two real machines exist: a chat's events reach only its own machine, a surface event for a chat on the second machine never lands on the first, and input for an offline machine is held and later flushed to that machine alone. Every later group's tests build on this rig, so it must be usable by them.

Unhappy paths: a daemon started with no registration; a daemon whose stored registration has been revoked; two daemons started from the same home directory; a directory request naming a path outside that machine's roots; a shell opened against a folder that does not exist on that machine; a root designated at a path that machine does not have; a root removed that was never designated. Each names the problem rather than falling through to somewhere that happens to work. The server owns minting a registration code, renaming a host, marking one the home host and revoking one, so those four go over HTTP even when the command is invoked on that machine (02-daemon.md ## Control IPC, 17-cli.md ## Hosts and the CLI).

name: Testing C1 (daemon machine identity and two-daemon rig)
Daemon — agent backends, per-machine credentials, and how a chat gets its model

tasks.task:
The daemon stops being wired directly to one agent and gains a backend concept.

A backend supplies four things: the models it can run, the credential those models authenticate with, the permission modes it accepts, and the transcript store it persists sessions to. The daemon reports the backends a machine has, and a chat's model selects the backend that runs it. The backend that exists is driven in-process against the machine's OWN installation of that agent rather than a bundled copy, so a turn runs on the same program, version and configuration the user gets in their own terminal, and the resolved location and version are reported for that machine.

The daemon provisions a backend the machine lacks rather than reporting it as missing. Present and usable: resolve it and report where it is and what version it is. Absent: install it through that backend's own installer, reporting progress to surfaces on the contract's component-progress channel. Present but logged out: report itself unauthenticated naming that backend, so settings can offer that backend's routes to a credential. A failed install is reported and turns for that backend are held until it is resolved, and it must not leave the machine looking provisioned. Backends are independent: a machine with one backend unprovisioned keeps running chats on the others.

Backend credentials are per machine and live on the machine that runs the turns. Each machine reports an account state per backend, and connecting, switching and disconnecting each act on one backend on one machine. The daemon accepts all three over the contract's per-machine, per-backend credential frames from a surface and over the matching endpoints on its own local socket, so the app and the command line drive one implementation. The existing credential rules stand and must not regress: the daemon's own store is authoritative after first boot, seeded once from the environment, then the backend's own credentials file, then the platform keystore, in that order; disconnecting empties that store without deleting it and without touching the backend's own credential; connecting either takes a pasted token or re-adopts whatever the backend already has on that machine; no surface ever holds a model key, and a raw model key is stripped from the environment a turn runs in.

Unhappy paths: a chat whose model belongs to a backend this machine has not provisioned, which cannot run and says exactly that; a credential operation aimed at a backend the machine does not have; a credential operation aimed at an offline machine, refused up front naming it rather than buffered to take effect minutes later; an install that fails.

Which model a chat runs on is resolved on the machine that will run it, not by whoever asked. Nothing owns this today, and every spawn site depends on it, so it is defined once here.

- A model named at spawn is fixed for that chat's life and selects the backend that runs it.
- A spawn may OMIT the model, and omitting it must work. The chat then runs on its machine's last-used model.
- A machine RECORDS the model of each chat spawned on it, so the last-used value follows the machine rather than the surface that asked. Two chats started from different surfaces move the same per-machine value.
- A machine that has never run a chat still has a last-used model: it takes one from the FIRST catalogue it reads successfully, the newest entry of that catalogue, so a freshly added machine runs its first chat without anybody choosing a model on it. That read needs a working credential, so a machine whose backend is provisioned but logged out has none until the credential is connected, and gets one as soon as it is.
- The machine REPORTS its last-used model in its self-description, absent while it has none, so surfaces can preselect it and agents can read it without guessing.
- The only case where a spawn naming no model is an error is a machine that has never successfully read a catalogue, and the error says exactly that rather than inventing a model.

The catalogue itself is read from each provisioned backend's own provider rather than hard-coded, cached per backend for its existing lifetime, and returned newest-first with each entry naming the backend that serves it. A missing or expired credential, or a bad response from one provider, is returned as an error against THAT backend while the models from backends that answered stay selectable. A catalogue already read is served for its lifetime even when a later refresh fails — caching a real read is not a fallback, inventing one is.

Unhappy paths: a spawn naming a model no provisioned backend offers; a catalogue read that fails on every backend; a machine whose only backend is logged out; two spawns racing on the same machine, which must leave one coherent last-used value rather than a torn one.

name: Testing C2 (agent backends and model resolution)
Daemon — permission mode as a setting at two scopes

tasks.task:
Turns still run without prompting by default — surfaces are remote and frequently asleep, and a prompt raised at three in the morning stalls everything that runs unattended — but the mode stops being a constant and becomes a setting the user controls at two scopes.

The effective mode resolves per turn: the chat's own override first, then its machine's default, then the no-prompting default. Both scopes are settable from any surface. The modes offered are the ones the chat's backend accepts, taken as that backend defines them rather than re-invented, so a machine whose backends differ offers different sets.

The daemon carries the effective mode on chat state so a surface can show the mode the NEXT turn will actually use, and it reports its own default plus how many of its chats carry an override in its self-description. Clearing a chat's override returns it to its machine's default, and the difference between "overridden to the same value the machine uses" and "not overridden" must survive a daemon restart.

A change takes effect on the next turn, not on the one already running.

Unhappy paths: a mode outside the set the backend accepts; a machine-default change aimed at an offline machine; a per-chat override on a chat whose backend is not provisioned; a chat whose stored override names a mode its backend no longer accepts.

name: Testing C3 (permission mode)
Daemon — optional components, per machine, driven from the app

tasks.task:
The large voice models stop shipping with anything and become per-machine downloads driven from the app.

Each machine advertises which optional components it has, each with its size and its state — not installed, downloading, installed, failed — plus progress and an error while those apply. Downloads are started and removed from a surface, against a named machine.

Progress streams live to every connected surface, so a download started from one surface is visible on the others, and the settled result lands on the machine's self-description rather than on the live progress stream, which is transient and never replayed. An interrupted download resumes rather than starting again, and a component counts as installed only once its size and digest verify.

The language environment those components need is created on the machine at that point rather than shipped in the artifact. The optional list holds the weights too large to put in every install — the speech synthesiser's and the local transcriber's. The small voice-activity model is not on that list: it is inside the daemon artifact already (A2), so everything depending on it works on every machine with nothing downloaded. A machine configured for remote speech-to-text installs nothing for it at all.

A machine that has the speech component installed warms it at boot so the first spoken reply does not pay the model load.

Unhappy paths: a component operation naming a component that machine does not offer; a download that runs out of disk; a digest that does not verify, which must NOT be marked installed; a remove while a session is using that component; any component operation aimed at an offline machine.

name: Testing C4 (optional components)
Daemon — self-update under the service manager

tasks.task:
A machine keeps its daemon current without anybody logging into it.

The daemon checks the server for a newer build when it boots and again on a schedule, downloads it, verifies it carries the project's signing identity, and restarts itself under the machine's own service manager. It also applies an update on demand when a surface asks it to, so a user who sees a stale machine can act on it.

A machine behind the current build says so in its self-description, which is what lets surfaces offer the control at all. A failed update leaves the running version in place and reports the failure to surfaces, rather than leaving a machine with nothing running on it.

Unhappy paths: a download that fails part-way; an artifact whose signature does not verify, which is refused rather than installed; a service manager that refuses the restart; an update check made while the server is unreachable, which is not an error state for the machine, just no update this time; an update asked for on a machine that is already current.

name: Testing C5 (daemon self-update)
Jobs and triggers addressed to a machine

tasks.task:
A job now says which machine its work happens on.

A folder-addressed action — spawning a fresh chat each fire, or ensuring one persistent chat exists — carries the machine as part of its address and stores it with the job, so the job fires on the machine it was written for however long later. It may also carry a model; a spawn carrying none has its model resolved on the machine it fires at. An action that messages an existing chat takes both machine and model from the chat it delivers into.

A folder-addressed action carries both the machine and the folder, and both are required: there is no machine-wide directory a job falls back to, so an action saved without either is rejected at the API rather than resolved to a guess.

Firing at an offline machine writes the action to that machine's own pending queue and flushes it when that machine reconnects, bounded as before, and the run log names the machine and shows the run as pending. A backlog belongs to one machine and does not touch another.

Everything that reads or writes a job carries the machine with it: the stored definition, the run log entry, the editor's data, and the tools an agent uses to create and edit jobs. An action that names a folder without the machine it is on is refused rather than sent to whichever machine happens to be attached; an action that names a machine without a folder on it is refused the same way. A caller that does not know which machine to name discovers one first from the machine list it already has a tool for, so no job is ever created against an address nobody chose.

Unhappy paths: a job naming a machine that has been removed; a job whose folder does not exist on the machine it names, which is a loud failure recorded against that run rather than a silent skip; a message action whose chat lives on a machine that is gone; a filter that passes but an action that cannot be addressed; an action saved with no folder, refused at the API and at every editor; several fires stacking up for one offline machine, which arrive as a backlog rather than as lost work.
spec_sections: 12-error-and-offline.md ### Cron fires while a host is down
12-error-and-offline.md ### Webhook arrives while a host is down

name: Testing D1 (jobs addressed to a machine)
Cross-machine addressing — relay a call to another machine, and let an agent find machines

tasks.task:
A cross-chat call may name a chat on a different machine from the one the calling agent is running on, and the system must carry it there and bring the answer back inside the turn.

A call whose target is on the calling chat's own machine is executed in place, as now. One naming another machine is relayed by the server to that machine and its response relayed back to the caller. Surfaces see the call either way, so cross-chat activity reads as an audit trail regardless of which machines were involved.

A call naming an offline machine returns an error to the calling agent naming that machine, within the turn. A tool result is part of a turn in progress, so it resolves rather than buffering the way a user's message does, and the agent decides what to do about the machine being down.

An agent must be able to resolve a machine the user names in words — "the laptop", "the always-on box" — to the identity that spawning a chat and creating a job both require. Nothing gives it that today, and a machine with no chats on it yet is invisible to every listing an agent has.

Give every chat's agent a way to list every registered machine, each with its id, its name, whether it is online, whether it is the account's home machine, and its last-used model. That listing is how an agent turns a human word into an address, so it must include a machine that has never run anything.

The chat-listing call likewise carries each chat's machine, so a folder path is never ambiguous between two of them. The voice-device listing is scoped the same way, and it is built by the voice group (H1) with the per-machine device register it reads.

Spawning from an agent names the machine and may name a model or leave it out; left out, the new chat's model is resolved on that machine.

Unhappy paths: a call naming a chat that exists on no machine; a call naming an offline machine; a call naming a machine that has been removed; a spawn naming a folder that does not exist on the machine named; a relayed call whose target machine drops mid-call, which must resolve as an error inside the turn rather than hang it.

name: Testing D2 (cross-machine relay and machine discovery)
The home machine, the special threads, and what removing a machine means

tasks.task:
The three singleton threads — the manager, the messaging-bot mirror and the speakers transcript — live on exactly one nominated machine, and which machine that is must be settable. Nobody owns changing it today.

The account has one home machine. It is set when the first machine registers, and changed from any surface's settings through a request naming the new one. Exactly one machine carries the marker; setting it on another moves it. Changing it creates the three thread folders and their empty, user-owned guidance files on the new machine and leaves the previous machine's transcripts readable where they are — nothing is migrated and nothing is deleted. The threads cannot exist on two machines at once, and a machine that is not the home machine does not create the thread folders.

The three thread folders are manager, telegram and speakers under a threads directory inside the daemon's own state directory, in the home directory of the user that daemon runs as, beside the per-chat state, credentials and local socket it already keeps there. They resolve from that user's home and nothing else, so a service the operating system starts at boot lands on the same three paths every time and no group has to decide what working directory the service unit carries. What a thread inherits is that user's own agent configuration, which the daemon already runs under, plus the command-line skill the installer writes there; anything beyond that goes in the thread's own guidance file. Inbound bot messages route to the home machine.

Because delivery is spread across machines and the threads that make sense of a reply are not on all of them, this group also moves the broadcast records off any machine's disk and onto the server, and owns both ends of that: the server appends a record as it routes an announcement on a channel one of these threads mediates, and the home machine's daemon reads the pending records when the user replies, injects them into that turn's prompt, and clears only the ones that turn consumed. Nothing is written by one machine for another machine to read. A record that arrives while the home machine is offline, or while it is mid-turn, is still there for the next reply, and pending records follow the threads when the home machine changes.

While the home machine is offline the three threads are unavailable and every surface says so plainly, rather than showing them as ordinary idle chats with a composer that appears to work.

Removing a machine is confirmed and names how many chats live on it; its registration is invalidated, its link dropped, its chats unreachable while their history stays on that machine, and every other machine carries on unaffected. Because exactly one machine carries the home marker, this group also DEFINES, once, what removing the home machine does to that marker, so no surface invents its own answer. It must not be possible, through any surface, to end up with a registered account and no home machine.

Unhappy paths: changing the home machine to one that is offline or unregistered, refused and naming it; a home-machine change while a thread is mid-turn, which must not lose that turn's transcript; an inbound bot message or a speaker announcement arriving while the home machine is offline, where the announcement is still recorded and reaches the thread's next reply; a reply whose agent invocation fails, which must leave the records pending rather than consuming them; removing the machine that is currently the home machine.

name: Testing D3 (home machine and special threads)
Web — Settings, Hosts, and adding a machine

tasks.task:
Settings gains the place where machines are watched and managed, replacing today's single-daemon section.

One row per machine. A row shows its name, editable in place; whether it is online or offline with its last heartbeat, stated exactly once; its platform; its daemon version with an update control when one is available; and its agent backends, each carrying that backend's version and its account state, or the controls to connect, switch and disconnect that one backend on that one machine.

Expanding a row gives that machine's permission-mode default, chosen from the modes its backends accept, alongside how many of its chats carry a per-chat override; its optional components, each with size, state and install and remove controls, showing live progress while a download runs; its project folders, with add and remove controls that write through to that machine and settle on its next registry push rather than on the click; the control that marks it the account's home machine; and the control that removes it, confirmed and naming its chat count.

State comes from the live reports, with a quiet loading state before a machine's first report arrives and a plainly reported failure rather than a control that looks like it worked. Pending states resolve on the next report, not on a matching value, and a report that says the opposite of what was asked surfaces as an error rather than silently sticking.

The section obeys the app's existing rules without exception: no explanatory prose under any control, a switch for a boolean with a label that does not flip, icon-only controls carrying a short hover name, the shared close and delete glyphs at their shared size, and no text below the minimum size.

Unhappy paths: a rename to an empty name; a project root added at a path that machine does not have, reported as that; a component, permission, credential or folder action aimed at an offline machine, refused up front naming it rather than appearing to work and taking effect minutes later; a machine whose first report has not arrived; an update control on a machine that is already current; removing the machine that is currently the home machine, which follows the one rule defined for that case.

Above the machine list sits the way a new machine is added.

Adding a machine asks the server for a single-use registration code and renders it both scannably and typeably — the same code either way, because some machines are reached by typing rather than by pointing a camera — together with the one-line install command for the target operating system. The installer on the machine being added is what redeems that code, so this screen mints nothing and resolves when that machine registers. The install command likewise comes from the server, which is its single source; the surface renders what the server gives it and never composes it from its own idea of the server's address or of how a build is named.

The pairing screen must not confuse the two values a person can arrive with: the short code from Link a device, which this browser redeems for its own credential, and the credential token from the command line's bootstrap, which is the first sign-in of an account with no linked surface yet. It names both, and rejects the registration code from Add host up front, since that one authorises a machine rather than a sign-in.

Unhappy paths: a registration code that expires unused; a registration that never completes; a request for the install command before the server has published anything; an install command shown for an operating system the server has no build for; the same machine paired twice, which must resolve to one machine rather than two.
spec_sections: 02-daemon.md ### Desktop app and the local daemon

name: Testing E1 (web hosts settings)
Web — chats that know which machine they are on

tasks.task:
Starting a chat now means choosing a machine and a folder on it.

The folder picker is one list grouped by machine: under each machine's name, that machine's configured project folders first, then folders seen in recent chats on it, then a clearly secondary field for an ad-hoc path on that machine, plus a browse tree that reads that machine's own directories with a breadcrumb once the user has drilled in. Picking a folder picks the machine, and that pair is what the spawn carries; it is fixed for the chat's life. The picker defaults to the last used machine-and-folder pair, a machine added later appears as soon as it registers, and an offline machine's group renders greyed with choosing from it reporting that it is offline rather than spawning.

The browsed filesystem is ALWAYS the selected machine's, never the filesystem of the machine this surface runs on, because a locally picked path is a path the chosen machine does not have.

The model picker sits beside the folder pill, in the same shape of control, in the new-chat setup row rather than the header. It loads the chosen machine's catalogue and offers it newest-first, preselecting the draft's model, else that machine's last-used. A backend that failed to answer shows its error in the picker while the models from backends that did answer stay selectable, and the chat can still be spawned while the catalogue is unavailable. The model is chosen before the first message and fixed after it; changing the chosen machine re-reads the catalogue for the new one. Only one of the two pop-ups is open at a time and both dismiss on a click outside and on escape.

Unhappy paths: a folder that exists on one machine and not on another; an ad-hoc path that turns out not to exist, which surfaces the machine's own error on send and keeps the typed message; a catalogue that fails to load on every backend; a machine chosen and then removed before the first message; a spawn attempted on an offline machine.

The new-chat chords resolve the same pair: the plain chord starts a chat on the current or most-recently-used machine and folder without opening the picker, and the shifted chord opens the picker (14-design-web.md ## Keyboard shortcuts).

The rest of the web app learns that chats live on different machines.

Chats group by machine and folder, so the same path on two machines stays two groups. A machine being unreachable is a first-class, explained state scoped to that machine's chats: the banner names it, says messages will be queued and sent when it reconnects, links through to that machine's settings row, and becomes app-level only when every machine is offline. Navigation stays fully available and the composer stays usable and queues, while spawning a new chat on an offline machine is refused up front because its folder cannot be checked. Only the controls that genuinely cannot be queued are visibly disabled, with the machine named.

The connection state model keeps two independent indicators — the link to the server, and presence per machine — and a chat's indicator reflects its own machine's presence. There is no offline flash on load: an unknown machine reads as quiet, not as broken. The diagnostics screen reports one line per registered machine, so a machine being down reads differently from the server being down and from a rejected credential.

Everything that touches files resolves against the chat's own machine: the diff editor, the file browser and its project-wide jump, and the saves they write. The terminal drawer opens a shell on the chat's machine, and on a not-yet-created chat opens on the machine chosen in the picker, showing the directory the machine reports it actually started in. The skill autocomplete asks the chat's own machine for that folder's skills. The batch view spans machines, each member row carrying its own, and a member whose machine is offline shows that rather than blocking the batch. While the home machine is offline the three special threads read as unavailable rather than as ordinary idle chats.

Unhappy paths: a chat whose machine has been removed; an editor save while the chat's machine is offline; a terminal opened on an offline machine; a queued message that must flush to its own machine and no other; a machine reconnecting while its banner is on screen.

The chat's Tools panel carries that chat's permission mode: the effective mode the next turn will use, and a picker offering the modes the chat's backend accepts. Choosing one sets the per-chat override through the per-chat settings frame; a Use host default option clears it by sending that frame with the field omitted (14-design-web.md ## Tools panel).

The Schedules screens name the machine each job runs on.

A spawn or ensure action picks its folder with the same machine-grouped picker the new-chat flow uses: under each machine's name, that machine's configured project folders first, then folders seen in existing chats on it, plus an ad-hoc path field for that machine. Picking a folder picks the machine, and that pair is what the action stores. A new job seeds the folder to the most-recently-used machine-and-folder pair, the same seed the new-chat picker uses, and to nothing at all when there is no such pair; a spawn or ensure action left with no folder or no machine is blocked in the client with a message that says so, matching the API's own rule. A message action takes its machine from the recipient chat.

The Skill dropdown is fetched for the action's target machine and folder, and an already-saved skill stays selectable while that list is loading or after it fails.

The job list and the runs panel name the machine each action addresses, so the same path on two machines reads as two jobs, and a fire waiting on an offline machine reads as pending against that machine.

Unhappy paths: a job whose machine has been removed, which still opens and edits rather than breaking the page; a machine that goes offline between picking its folder and saving; a skill list that fails to load for the chosen machine; a saved job whose stored folder no longer exists on the machine it names.

name: Testing E2 (web machine-aware chat UX)
Desktop — make this Mac a machine, and sign what ships

tasks.task:
The desktop app is a surface that can also turn the machine it runs on into a host.

It offers to run a daemon here, installs it as an ordinary operating-system service with its own lifetime, shows that machine's status alongside every other machine's, and can restart it. Being linked already, it asks the server for the registration code itself and hands it to the daemon it just installed, so nobody types a code into the machine they are sitting at. The daemon it installs is not a child of the app: closing the app leaves it running, exactly as any other machine's daemon runs without a surface attached.

Being a host changes nothing about the app's role as a surface. It still browses the SELECTED machine's filesystem through the same in-app tree the browser app uses — never an operating-system directory dialog — even when the selected machine happens to be the one it is running on.

The shell is signed with the project's own signing identity rather than a vendor developer identity; notarisation stays off and builds are installed by direct copy so nothing is quarantined. Signing is what makes the shell's own update path work at all, and a publish refuses to proceed when the identity is missing or the built bundle is unsigned. The existing packaging and runtime invariants — the bootstrap running when packaged, the tray asset shipping inside the bundle, the single main-window owner, the menu-bar heartbeat driven from the imperative call sites, and readiness-gated messages into the renderer — must all keep holding.

Unhappy paths: an install attempt on a machine that already has a daemon, which adopts it rather than duplicating it; an install needing a permission the user declines; a daemon that installs but never pairs; a publish attempted with no signing identity; a shell that cannot reach its update feed.
spec_sections: 02-daemon.md ### Desktop app and the local daemon

name: Testing E3 (desktop local daemon and signing)
Mobile — machines at parity

tasks.task:
The phone app carries everything machine-shaped in settings.

Settings gains a hosts section: one row per machine with its name, its status shown exactly once, its daemon version and its update control, opening a sub-screen for that machine carrying its permission-mode default, its optional components with size, state and live progress where a download started here runs on that machine, its project folders with add and remove controls writing through to that machine, the control marking it the home machine, and removing it, confirmed and naming its chat count. Adding a machine asks the server for a registration code, shows it scannably and typeably beside the one-line install command the server gives it, and resolves when the machine being added redeems that code.

Backend accounts are shown per machine, one row per backend, with live state and connect, switch and disconnect controls. Switching accounts must be possible from a phone: the machine's own terminal is out of reach from there, so pasting a token is the only route to a different account and it must exist here.

The section obeys the app's existing rules: no descriptive subtitle under any section header, one spacing scale, the top safe-area inset applied through the shared wrapper, the display face for titles, and both colour schemes resolving real values on every control.

Unhappy paths: a component, credential or folder action aimed at an offline machine, refused up front naming it; a project root added at a path that machine does not have, reported as that; a machine whose first report has not arrived, which reads as loading rather than as disconnected; a rename to an empty name; removing the machine that is currently the home machine, following the one rule defined for that case.

The chat screen also carries the per-chat permission override, the second of the two scopes 02-daemon.md § Permission mode says every surface sets: the effective mode the next turn will use, a picker of the modes that chat's backend accepts, and a Use host default option that clears the override by sending chat.settings with the field omitted.

The phone app's chat side learns about machines.

The new-chat folder browser opens at each machine's roots, grouped and labelled by machine, and drills into one machine's tree with a breadcrumb that appears only once the user has drilled in. Folder names are the primary label with the full path as muted secondary text, recently-used and machine-published folders sit at the top as one-tap shortcuts defaulting to the last used machine-and-folder pair, and an offline machine's group renders greyed with choosing from it reporting that it is offline. Picking a folder picks the machine, and that pair is what the spawn carries. A new chat spawns naming no model, resolved on the chosen machine, and the phone offers no model control at all.

A machine being offline is a first-class banner that names it, scoped to that machine's chats and going app-level only when every machine is offline, with a tap-through to that machine's settings row. Navigation stays available, the composer stays usable and queues, spawning on an offline machine is refused, and only the ephemeral-audio controls are visibly disabled with the machine named. The diagnostics screen lists one line per registered machine and stays reachable from both banners.

Unhappy paths: an offline machine chosen in the picker; a chat on a machine that has been removed; a queued message flushed to its own machine and no other; a machine whose presence is still unknown, which must not flash as offline on launch.

The phone's Schedules editor reaches the same parity on machines.

A spawn or ensure action picks its folder with the machine-grouped folder browser the new-chat flow uses, so picking a folder picks the machine and that pair is what the action stores. A message action takes its machine from the recipient chat, and the Skill dropdown is fetched for the action's target machine and folder. Saving a spawn or ensure action with no folder or no machine is blocked with a message that says so, matching the API's own rule, and the inline Schedules list on the Settings tab names the machine each job addresses.

Unhappy paths: a job whose machine has been removed; a machine that goes offline between picking its folder and saving; a skill list that fails to load for the chosen machine.

name: Testing F1 (mobile machines)
Command line — machines as a resource, and this machine as the default

tasks.task:
The command line gains machines as a first-class resource and a default that matches where it is run. Its own spec now owns the whole command-line surface as one list — the surface, terminal-design and daemon documents each defer to it instead of restating a partial set, and the entries that used to live only in those documents (attaching to a live chat, resuming one, printing a transcript, revoking a linked surface, obtaining the first credential, opening a pairing code for another surface) are in that one list under their resource group. Where any document disagrees with it, it wins. Every command in that list is this group's to build, and the list is what decides that — a command is not skipped here for being absent from the summary below. The families whose data another group owns print what that group stores: jobs and their run logs name the machine each action addresses (D1), and the threads family names the home machine the three threads run on (D3).

The hosts family is every entry under hosts in 17-cli.md § Commands. Reaching every machine-scoped control the graphical surfaces have is that family's floor, so no machine setting is reachable from web or phone and not from here, and an entry with no graphical counterpart is built here just the same. It lists every registered machine with its name, status, version and components; shows one in full including its platform, its backends and their versions, its components, its permission-mode default and whether it carries the home marker; asks the server for a registration code and prints it scannably and typeably beside the server's install command, for the new machine's installer to redeem; renames one; MARKS ONE THE ACCOUNT'S HOME MACHINE; sets one's permission-mode default; lists, adds to and removes from one's project-folder registry; reads one's model catalogue; connects, switches and disconnects one backend's credential on one machine, the paste-a-token route included; installs AND REMOVES an optional component on one; applies an available daemon update to one; and removes one, confirmed and naming its chat count.

Every one of those subcommands accepts an explicit machine and defaults to the machine the command is invoked on — none is restricted to it. Removal is the single exception: it requires the machine to be named, so an irreversible revocation is never aimed by default.

The per-chat permission override is settable here too, the second of the two scopes every surface sets.

Removing the machine that is currently the home machine follows the single rule defined for that case, identically to every other surface; the command line does not invent its own answer.

Two flags name two different things and must never be conflated: one names the SERVER to talk to and flips the tool into remote mode; the other names a MACHINE to act on. The default machine for any command is the one it is invoked on, so starting a chat in a folder there runs there and talks to that machine's daemon over its local socket, presenting the key it reads from where that daemon keeps it. Addressing another machine is explicit, accepts either a name or the leading part of an id, and routes through the server instead of the local socket.

Starting a chat may name a model or leave it out; left out, the model is resolved on the target machine. The interactive picker lists recent folders grouped by machine with this machine first. A non-interactive start validates the folder against the target machine and errors loudly when it is not there, with folder completion asked of the target machine so it works whichever machine the command line itself is on. Every machine-scoped command aimed at THIS machine goes over that machine's local socket, which carries one endpoint per host-scoped control for exactly that reason; opening the adoption window for a voice device is the one machine command that exists only there and takes no machine flag, because the daemon adopts the device itself and nothing in that exchange crosses the server. This group builds that command and the socket endpoint that opens the window; what the window then does with a device that announces itself belongs to the voice group (H1). The daemon subcommands remain for manual service control now that the installer registers the service, and status reports the daemon's version. Log tailing is per machine, and diagnostics reports per-machine status and each machine's pending backlog.

The surface stays single-resource operations only. What it deliberately does not carry is stated rather than left as a hole: transcript- and editor-shaped gestures belong to the surfaces that render them, and registering an Android push token can only be done by the device holding it. The machine-readable output mode stays the contract agents drive it through, and the agent-facing skill that teaches this surface is updated to match the full list. That skill ships inside the daemon artifact and the installer writes it into each machine's own agent skills directory, so it reaches every chat on that machine including the three special threads, rather than only chats started beneath one particular repository.

Unhappy paths: a machine value that is ambiguous or unknown, which is an error listing the candidates rather than a guess; a local command run on a machine with no daemon, which says so rather than hanging; a machine named after it has been removed; an operation needing a live link to an offline machine, refused naming it. The server owns minting a registration code, renaming a host, marking one the home host and revoking one, so those four go over HTTP even when the command is invoked on that machine (02-daemon.md ## Control IPC, 17-cli.md ## Hosts and the CLI).

The chats, jobs, hooks, threads and surfaces command families, every invocation in 17-cli.md ## Commands, each with its --json shape. A command is delivered or it is reported missing; absence from a summary is not a reason to skip one.
The interactive picker, the --server/--host flag split, patch doctor, and the patch-cli skill shipped alongside the artifact.

name: Testing G1 (command line machines)
Voice bound to a machine

tasks.task:
Voice becomes something that happens on a particular machine.

A chat's voice runs on that chat's own machine: the surface opens its audio session against that machine, and speaking to a chat requires the speech components to be installed there. Voice is therefore a per-machine capability rather than a property of the product.

A surface disables a voice affordance whose component is missing on the machine in question and names both the machine and what is needed. Pressing it asks once, in a single prompt naming the download size and the machine, and on accept starts that machine's download with progress shown in place; declining cancels the action and starts nothing. A machine whose speech backend is remote installs nothing for it and still works.

A physical speaker device belongs to one machine, adopted by that machine's own daemon inside a five-minute window that machine's command line opens on it (G1 builds that command and the socket endpoint behind it). This group builds what the window does: it stays open five minutes, the first device to announce itself inside it is recorded and its control link accepted from then on, an announcement outside a window is refused, and re-pairing moves a device to another machine. Nothing in that exchange reaches the server, because the device carries no account credential; the per-session voice token stays server-minted as it is for every other surface, fetched by the daemon on the device's behalf. An announcement addressed to speakers is therefore relayed to the machine those devices belong to — not to the calling chat's machine — and that machine synthesises and speaks it. The device listing an agent reads is this group's too, scoped to the calling chat's own machine and answered from that machine's own device register. The existing cascade for choosing a device, and its fall-through when none can be reached, is unchanged apart from being resolved on the devices' own machine, and its last step hands the message back to the server as an ordinary push notification rather than that machine reaching the push provider itself.

The machine that speaks an announcement writes no record of it. The record the speakers thread reads when the user replies is written by the server as it routes the announcement (09-notifications.md), so this group delivers and leaves the log alone.

Unhappy paths: opening voice against a chat whose machine is offline; opening voice against a machine with the component missing; a speaker announcement whose devices' machine is offline, which continues down the existing cascade to its fallback; a component removed while a session is live; more concurrent sessions on one machine than it can carry.

name: Testing H1 (voice per machine)
Deployment split, environment split, and versions across every machine

tasks.task:
Deployment splits into a server that is deployed and a daemon that is installed.

The reference deployment carries the server and its reverse proxy only. The daemon is no longer part of that stack and is no longer a container. A machine may run both, in which case the daemon reaches the server over loopback and the shared data directory stays owned by the user the daemon runs as. Sizing guidance follows the split: a machine running voice needs the headroom voice needs, and a machine on remote speech-to-text with no components installed needs only what the daemon and the agent's own work need.

The environment splits accordingly: the speech-backend selection, its key, and the agent-backend credential seed are read by the daemon and belong in each machine's service environment rather than in the server's. Everything else stays the server's.

Building splits too. Deploying means running the server, which builds and serves the web app with it. The daemon, the desktop app and the phone app are builds a person installs, and the daemon build publishes its artifacts to the server so one channel feeds both a new machine's install and every machine's self-update. A server deploy completes without touching any machine: every daemon's link drops and each one restores itself, and chats in flight during the restart surface the drop rather than hanging.

Version reporting now covers five independently delivered layers, and the daemon layer differs from machine to machine. Every layer is stamped from one source of truth, clients report themselves on connect, and the version report names every layer, every linked device, every machine's daemon and any drift between them with a remedy per item. An unstamped or unreadable layer reads as unknown rather than as agreement, a malformed report is rejected at the client boundary rather than rendering as "everything agrees", and a delivery that leaves the deployment inconsistent fails.

Bring the repository's own deploy recipe into line: it must stop describing the daemon as part of the compose stack, and its verification steps must check the server and each machine's link rather than a container. Cutting the existing single-daemon installation over is a clean re-pair, not a migration — write no migration code, and make sure nothing in the deploy path assumes pre-existing chats, jobs or buffered payloads are carried across. The recipe links a surface before it adds the machine, because the registration code comes from a linked surface and there is nothing to give an installer until one exists. Every step and every check the recipe names is an existing command from 17-cli.md § Commands, built by G1 — the first credential, the per-machine status the verification reads, and re-pairing each voice device to the host that carries its components, which is the one cutover step no graphical surface can perform. The recipe invents no command of its own.

Unhappy paths: a deploy that leaves the web app behind the server; a machine reporting a version outside the range the server supports; a layer that cannot be read; a daemon publish that half-completes; a verification step that would pass against a stale artifact.
The daemon publish channel and the version reporting each layer contributes, end to end.
The deploy recipe brought into line with the split stack, inventing no command the CLI does not already provide.

name: Testing I1 (deployment split and version reporting)
The spec-to-test index, rebuilt against the finished system

tasks.task:
The traceability index — the matrix mapping every spec file to the tests that cover its claims — lives with the engineering documentation rather than beside the spec, and it must describe the system as it now is rather than as it was before this change.

Rebuild it against the finished build: every spec file, its key claims including all the machine-shaped ones added here, and the tests that actually cover each. Status is marked honestly, and every remaining gap is named rather than papered over — a claim with no test is recorded as uncovered, and a test that only covers part of a claim says which part. Anything that can only be checked by a person, or only by the toolchain rather than at runtime, is marked as such rather than counted as covered.
